item.title: Spring AI
item.description:
Spring AI is a Spring project for building applications that use generative-AI models. It provides portable Java interfaces for model access and Spring Boot auto-configuration for model providers, vector stores, tool calling, conversation memory, retrieval augmented generation, observability, evaluation, and the Model Context Protocol.

Spring AI does not contain a language model. It connects an application to a remote or local model:

text 
Spring application
 -> Spring AI ChatClient / model API
 -> provider SDK or HTTP API
 -> OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Amazon, Azure, Ollama, or another provider

Its role is similar to Spring Data’s role for databases: application code uses common concepts while provider adapters handle transport and provider-specific details. The abstraction reduces coupling, but providers are not identical. Model names, token limits, structured-output behavior, tool support, safety controls, and request options still vary.

item.title: Spring Environment and Profiles
item.description:
Spring’s Environment combines two concerns: resolving configuration properties and determining which bean-definition profiles are active. The core framework defines the abstraction and standard JVM/servlet sources; Spring Boot adds its own external-configuration sources and precedence rules.

Property Sources and Precedence #

A configurable environment owns ordered PropertySource<?> objects in MutablePropertySources. Resolution searches from highest to lowest precedence and returns the first source containing the requested key. item.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle and Prototype Scope
item.description:
Spring separates bean metadata from bean instances. A BeanDefinition describes how to create an object, while a BeanFactory applies that definition when the object is requested. An ApplicationContext adds coordinated startup, post-processing, events, resource loading, and shutdown.

What Happens During Context Refresh #

AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() prepares the environment and bean factory before application singletons become usable. The major stages are:

  1. Prepare or obtain the BeanFactory and load bean definitions.
  2. Invoke BeanFactoryPostProcessors, including configuration-class processing, while definitions can still be changed.
  3. Discover and register BeanPostProcessors.
  4. Initialize context infrastructure such as message resolution, events, and context-specific resources.
  5. Instantiate the remaining non-lazy singleton beans.
  6. Publish the refreshed state and ContextRefreshedEvent.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor changes metadata. A BeanPostProcessor instead sees instances and can inject fields, invoke lifecycle annotations, or replace a bean with a proxy. Creating ordinary application beans from a factory post-processor is unsafe because it can instantiate them before all post-processors are registered.

item.title: Spring Annotation Processing
item.description:
Spring uses annotations as declarative metadata for component discovery, configuration, dependency injection, transactions, web request mapping, and other framework services. Java reflection exposes the raw annotations; Spring adds a consistent model for composed annotations, aliases, search strategies, and metadata reading without loading classes.

Java Annotation Semantics #

An annotation declaration is itself an interface whose implicit superinterface is java.lang.annotation.Annotation:

java 
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface Audited {
}

Runtime reflection can inspect @Audited when it is directly present on a class. Meta-annotations such as @Retention, @Target, and @Documented describe an annotation declaration but do not cause arbitrary transitive lookup.

item.title: Spring Overview and Transactions
item.description:
Spring Framework provides a dependency-injection container plus focused modules for AOP, data access, transactions, messaging, and web applications. Transaction management demonstrates the framework’s integration model: application code declares a boundary, while an interceptor coordinates a resource-specific PlatformTransactionManager or reactive transaction manager.

Proxy-Based Declarative Transactions #

With the default advice mode, Spring wraps an eligible bean in an AOP proxy. Calls entering a method matched by @Transactional pass through TransactionInterceptor, which reads transaction metadata, starts or joins a transaction, invokes the target, and commits or rolls back.

item.title: Project Reactor
item.description:
Project Reactor is a Java library for composing asynchronous and event-driven programs. Its core types, Mono<T> and Flux<T>, describe computations that may produce values later rather than returning those values immediately.

Reactor is the reactive foundation used by Spring WebFlux. It is also useful outside HTTP servers for asynchronous clients, event streams, messaging, concurrent orchestration, and any pipeline whose inputs may arrive over time.

item.title: Spring Resources
item.description:
org.springframework.core.io.Resource gives Spring APIs one handle for content that may reside in a file, classpath entry, URL, servlet context, byte array, or already-open stream. The abstraction describes access capabilities; it does not make every resource seekable, repeatable, writable, or backed by a file.

The Resource Contract #

Resource extends InputStreamSource. getInputStream() is the fundamental operation, while methods such as exists(), isReadable(), isOpen(), isFile(), contentLength(), lastModified(), and getDescription() expose capabilities or metadata.

item.title: Spring Container Types
item.description:
Spring’s container API has three distinct layers: bean metadata, the factory that creates objects from that metadata, and an application context that coordinates the factory with application services. Keeping those layers separate makes Spring source code and extension points easier to reason about.

Bean Definitions and Registries #

BeanDefinition is mutable metadata for one bean. It records the bean class or class name, scope, constructor arguments, property values, qualifiers, factory method, lifecycle methods, role, source location, and explicit dependencies. The parent/child metadata relationship is independent of Java inheritance.

item.title: Spring Conversion and Validation
item.description:
Spring treats conversion, presentation formatting, object binding, and validation as separate operations. A request parameter can therefore become a typed property and still produce structured errors without coupling the domain object to a web controller.

Conversion and Formatting #

ConversionService is the facade for type conversion. It can first answer whether a conversion is available and then convert by raw class or by TypeDescriptor, which preserves annotations and nested generic information.

item.title: Spring MVC
item.description:
Spring MVC is the Servlet-based web framework in Spring Framework. Its front controller, DispatcherServlet, coordinates request mapping, argument resolution, controller invocation, return-value handling, and exception translation. Spring WebFlux uses a different reactive runtime and threading model; the two frameworks must not be treated as interchangeable.

Bootstrap and Dispatch #

A non-Boot Servlet application can register a web application context and dispatcher through WebApplicationInitializer:

java 
public final class WebInitializer implements WebApplicationInitializer {
 @Override
 public void onStartup(ServletContext servletContext) {
 var context = new AnnotationConfigWebApplicationContext();
 context.register(WebConfiguration.class);

 var servlet = servletContext.addServlet(
 "mvc", new DispatcherServlet(context));
 servlet.setLoadOnStartup(1);
 servlet.addMapping("/");
 }
}

Spring Boot performs equivalent registration for an MVC application. Mapping the dispatcher to / lets the Servlet container retain special handling for static resources and JSPs; /* also captures those dispatches.

item.title: Spring Thread Pools
item.description:
Spring’s TaskExecutor abstracts task submission. The common ThreadPoolTaskExecutor is a managed JavaBean wrapper around ThreadPoolExecutor; its pool, queue, rejection, and lifecycle choices still determine system capacity.

Defining and Naming an Executor #

Name executors by workload so callers select the intended resource:

java 
@Bean("reportExecutor")
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor reportExecutor() {
 var executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
 executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
 executor.setMaxPoolSize(24);
 executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
 executor.setKeepAliveSeconds(30);
 executor.setThreadNamePrefix("report-");
 executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(
 new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
 return executor;
}

Spring initializes and shuts down a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor as a managed bean. Returning its concrete type preserves lifecycle configuration and monitoring methods. Separate executors isolate workloads with different latency, blocking, priority, or downstream-capacity requirements.

item.title: Spring Data JPA Specification API
item.description:
When a Spring Data JPA repository needs a WHERE clause that is optional, composable, and decided at runtime, the usual API is org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaSpecificationExecutor<T>.

It is the bridge between:

  1. Spring Data repository methods such as findAll(...), count(...), and exists(...)
  2. Spring’s org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.Specification<T>
  3. the Jakarta Persistence Criteria API centered around jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaBuilder

JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> #

Suppose we have an entity:

java 
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class PurchaseOrder {
 @Id
 private Long id;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String status;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private String customerEmail;

 @Column(nullable = false)
 private Instant createdAt;

 @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
 private Customer customer;
}
